title: Ayeuonganit Aunakésuck Muhhogkunk
summary: Ayeuonganit Aunakésuck Muhhogkunk, also known as Burying Point, is a now desecrated 18th century Montaukett burying ground and arrowhead workshop. Both traditional stone grave markers and contemporary headstones were found and moved from the area for residential development.
activity_update_summary: Consolidated dated history into the cited Historic Timeline so the listing no longer repeats the same content.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: This eighteenth-century Montaukett burying ground, whose Algonquian name translates to "In this place, they painted the dead," was tragically desecrated when developers removed its traditional stone markers to build residential homes. Acknowledging this profound spatial violation highlights the ongoing vulnerability of Native resting places and underscores the critical, modern need to aggressively protect sacred Indigenous landscapes from erasure.
translation_content:
Ayeuonganit Aunakésuck Muhhogkunk translates to 'In this place, they painted the dead.'

Ayeuonganit (n.) - to the place, from ayeau - he is located, he is in this or that place.

Aunakésuck (Narragansett v. pl.) - they are painted.

Muhhogkunk (n. collection pl., an indef. nubmer of) dead bodies. 1

The contemporary name for this cemetery is Burying Place Point, however for the project, it has been renamed for it's unique feature of commercial house paint found in the graves which used in substitution for red ochre that served as a traditional and ceremonial function
artifacts_content: Artifacts associated with the graves included 6,000 purple quahog and white whelk wampum beads in a belt or vest over the upper half of the body; a necklace of 255 wampum beads, and some made from the stem of a kaolin pipe; and "goose-head" shaped purple quahog shell heads; 32 copper buttons; three pewter buttons; twenty tiny copper tubular heads; minute brass and shell disk beads; striped red and blue, black, and clear glass beads; a brass ring; a small brass chain; a bone knife handle; a copper pail; two spines of dogfish, and the skeleton of a small dog. [1. Southold Indian Museum catalog, "contact grave-Montauk," Box 380, 1-203, 47]
vandalism_content: In 1928, archaeologist Roy Latham discovered graves after they had been partially destroyed by the developer and vandalized by people of Amagansett who had run off with two copper buckets, spoons, and other large articles.[Gaynell Stone, The History and Archaeology of the Montauk Vol 3, 1993 pp. 608] Both traditional stone grave markers and contemporary headstones were found and moved from the area for residential development. [1. Jeannette Edwards Rattray, Montauk - Three Centuries of Sport and Adventure, 1938 pp. 13]
